newsitem.title: UK: Eurostar float plans unscathed by fire - chairman.
newsitem.headline: Eurostar float plans unscathed by fire - chairman.

text.p: London and Continental Railways, owner of the Channel Tunnel passenger train service Eurostar, said on Thursday that the recent fire which swept through the tunnel would not hit its own plans for a billion stg flotation.

Plans for the float remained on track, said Sir Derek Hornby, chairman of LCR. The flotation is due to happen within the next 18 months, with the group planning to release initial plans next summer, when it produces accounts for Eurostar to the year ending December 31.
But, Hornby said there had been a short-term impact on passenger numbers after the fire.
Hornby made the comments at a London press briefing to mark the clearance of UK legislation for the 2.8 billion stg Channel Tunnel Rail Link, which will be built by the LCR consortium.

Construction of the link, one of the biggest civil engineering projects this century, kicks off in 1998. It will be funded partly by Eurostar flotation proceeds, with the remaining funding coming from bank finance and possibly revenues from the passenger service itself.
Commenting on the tunnel fire, he said: "We haven't made any alteration to our plans. We see this fire as an isolated case. But after the fire, passenger figures were down."
But Eurostar says passenger numbers have picked up recently, with Thursday's traffic at 10,000 people, compared with pre-fire levels of 12,000 passengers "on a good day" said Hornby.
Eurostar is remaining silent about the level of compensation it expects to receive from Eurotunnel, the Channel Tunnel owner and operator.

The passenger train capacity is running at 90 percent. But, the chairman said that for 14 days after the fire on November 18 the trains were completely out-of-action. He said it was impossible to evaluate the total level of its claim against Eurotunnel as services were still not back to normal.

Turning to the rail link itself, legislation is now in place for plans to proceed. The link will be capable of running high-speed trains to the Channel Tunnel at Folkestone, with a maximum speed of 186 miles per hour.
It is seen cutting travel to continental destinations by 35 minutes, with the London to Brussels journey seen at two hours and London to Paris within two hours and 15 minutes.
The terms of the UK legislation will allow foreign high-speed train operators to also run their trains along the link in return for a fee to LCR.
The LCR consortium includes coach company National Express Group, UK entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group, SBC Warburg, London Electricity and engineering group Bechtel.
